results.title: Mineworkers’ Union denies Land Ministry’s claim of consultation on contract mining
results.content: The Ghana Mineworkers’ Union (GMWU) has rejected claims by the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources that it has held extensive consultations with the Union over the government’s directives on contract mining. In a statement issued on Thursday, October 22, 2026, the Union described the Ministry’s assertion in a press release dated October 21 as “factually inaccurate”. The GMWU said it petitioned the Ministry on August 20 after raising concerns about the Local Content Policy, particularly its implications for contract mining and workers’ conditions.

The four-member delegation, led by Ghana’s Ambassador to Côte d’Ivoire, Alhassan Abu, visited the facility on Monday, October 12, 2026, according to a statement from the Embassy. results.title: Obuasi SHTS headmaster assault linked to alleged fetus burial, not sexual abuse – Apaak
results.content: Deputy Education Minister Dr Clement Apaak has clarified that an earlier incident involving the headmaster of Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS) concerned allegations of a fetus burial on the school premises, not sexual abuse. Speaking on JoyNews’ News Night on Thursday, October 22, 2026, Dr Apaak said the incident, which reportedly led to students assaulting the headmaster, was separate from the sexual abuse allegations that have since emerged. “It is important to indicate that while there is a report about an incident in the same school involving the same headmaster, that report was in relation to allegations of the burial of a fetus, which was said to have generated a reaction from a section of the students, leading to an assault on this very same headmaster,” he said.

In a press release issued on Thursday, October 22, 2026, and signed by its Head of Public Relations, Daniel Fenyi, the Service said preparations were far advanced for the resumption of academic work. results.title: Ghana’s hospitals are adopting AI, but the machines were never trained on Ghanaian patients
results.content: An algorithm that reads chest X-rays learns by looking at tens of thousands of them. It learns what a normal lung looks like, what tuberculosis looks like, what a tumour looks like, by being shown examples until the pattern sticks. The question nobody asks at the point of purchase is whose lungs it was shown. If the answer is Boston and Berlin and Seoul, and the lung now in front of it belongs to a farmer in Bolgatanga, the machine is working from a reference population that does not include him. It will still return an answer. It will return it with the same confident interface and the same clean percentage it would give a patient in Massachusetts. It just has a higher chance of being wrong, and nothing on the screen will tell the clinician which case this is.

results.title: Ghanaian clinic stored patient records on an unassessed system before regulator intervened
results.content: I spend part of my week in a laboratory and part of it behind a news desk. On the laboratory side, I sign out results. A full blood count. A fasting glucose. A hepatitis B surface antigen that will change how a patient is treated for the rest of their life. The moment I release that result, it stops being a piece of paper. It becomes a row in a database. It travels. It is stored somewhere, by someone, under terms I have never been shown. In nine years of laboratory practice, I have rarely seen a patient told where that information goes, who can see it, or what they are entitled to ask about it.
